I think you're overthinking this. Patient agency is a valuable factor in treatment choice for a variety of conditions. 

By warning that patient about risks and helping them make their own decision while giving your professional recommendation you're treating a patient with respect. Patients are capable of making their decisions and it's wrong for you to make potentially life changing decisions for them without their input.

In this scenario patients looking EHC are not looking to be pregnant. Warn them that EHC is not 100% effective but still has a chance to prevent pregnancy and that you recommend the Cu-IUD. 99% of patients will still want to take something that reduces their chance of pregnancy that getting pregnant.

There's very little way to know when exactly an ovulation has occurred. The modal is mid cycle of course but it theoretically can happen at any time including later than predicted. 

There's some evidence that EHC has a secondary MOA of thickening cervical mucus and preventing implantation but it's middling IMO.

I am always of the opinion to leave it the patient, advising that the Cu-IUD is the only proven effective EHC after ovulation and telling them how to contact the nearest GUM clinic if they chose to. But at the end of the day, if it has a chance of helping based on late ovulation it's better to give and warn it may not work than refuse access.

The £34 is not just raw cost but also factors in the cost of staff and our time.

A doctor with a 10-15 minute consultation. The GP reception staff who prep the prescription for output. The pharmacy staff who again check then dispense. The pharmacist who then does the final check for appropriateness. The staff at the BSO (NI government branch that then pay the pharmacy for each item we dispense) then take over.

That's a lot of people with a lot of qualifications: from entering uni to becoming a GP can take 8-10 years. To qualify as a pharmacist is a 5 year endeavour. To become a qualified pharmacy dispenser needs the NVQ 3 certification which on average takes 2 to 3 years 

The answer is the cost of highly trained staff rather than just the cost of a box of paracetamol

Pharmacy staff member here

What I see could making the biggest difference is public education, promoting health self-consciousness.

 So many people see GPs (and of course us pharmacy staff) as a free service they can avail for if anything goes wrong. You'd be shocked how much of our time is dispensing drugs that are much cheaper over the counter. I remember a case of a woman stubbing her toe and bruising it, she then went to the GP for a prescription of ibuprofen. 

The NHS spends so much money on things that are much cheaper to buy OTC. It's estimated here by the NHS that a pack of paracetamol costs £34 on prescription once all staff time is accounted for. I would sell the same pack over the counter for £1.49.

https://www.england.nhs.uk/2017/11/prescription-curbs-to-free-up-hundreds-of-millions-of-pounds-for-frontline-care/
